title: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VI, “A Note on Adsorption”; topic “Adsorption and membrane formation”. Scope: cell-walls and membranes of protozoa, plant cells and blood corpuscles

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch06-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Surface enrichment and mechanics are measurable, but the historical assertion that secretion is 'nothing more' than adsorption is unusually broad. Existing imaging and proteomics resolve components of the model, with serious causal confounding.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure whether membrane or wall constituents enrich at the surface according to their effects on interfacial tension and whether enrichment predicts increased local viscosity and rigidity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Adsorption, active trafficking, and biosynthetic secretion can produce similar enrichment.

Datasets seldom include interfacial tension and rigidity in the same cells.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open imaging can test the strong claim that a wall is nothing more than equilibrium adsorption, because vesicular delivery is visible in well-studied cells. The Gibbs-Thomson premise itself, that the accumulated molecules are there because they lower surface tension, is not a field in those image sets. Model plants and yeasts are adequate; the full scope across protozoa and corpuscles is not.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track where wall or membrane material first accumulates and whether that accumulation follows surface activity, as the Gibbs adsorption rule requires, or arrives by vesicular delivery. Accumulation of tension-lowering constituents at a free surface without exocytosis would support the claim; wall polymers delivered by vesicles on a biosynthetic timetable would refute the strong adsorption-only reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
These archives record trafficking and localization far more often than surface tension or adsorbability of the deposited molecules.

Blood-corpuscle membranes and protozoan cyst walls are poorly represented relative to model plant and fungal walls.
